slides.title: Subspace Products Retrieved
slides.notes: Open the lecture by making the retrieval theme explicit. Appendix C is not adding a new product; it is showing that the geometric product already contains the familiar subspace operations, provided we inspect the right grade component and remember the metric and duality conventions.

slides.title: The Retrieval Contract
slides.notes: Present these equations as the contract for the whole deck. The notation says: multiply first, then select the grade that has the geometric meaning wanted. Students should notice that invalid target grades are not errors; they are zero contributions in the same algebraic bookkeeping.

slides.title: Product Spectrum Before Selection
slides.notes: Slow down here because this is the conceptual hinge. The geometric product may contain several grades at once, so the grade selector acts like a mathematical filter. This lets one computation support exterior spanning, metric comparison, and contraction without pretending those meanings are interchangeable.

slides.title: Grade Support Map
slides.notes: Use the table as a sanity device, not as a memorization burden. If a grade request lies outside the available range, the selection is zero. The notebook turns this rule into a finite oracle, checking all basis-blade pairs in a small algebra.

slides.title: Worked Example: Split A Vector-Plane Product
slides.notes: Walk through this example carefully. The same product aB produces a grade-one contraction and a grade-three exterior component. Multiplying those retrieved pieces by the blade inverse turns them into the familiar vector projection e1 and rejection 2e3, so the diagram matches the algebra.

slides.title: Join And Meet From The Same Retrieval Habit
slides.notes: Connect this slide to earlier meet and join ideas without changing conventions midstream. The join is the top-grade exterior part when independence allows it. The meet is retrieved indirectly: dualize to constraints, join those constraints, and dualize back to the represented intersection.

slides.title: Projection And Rejection Pipeline
slides.notes: Use this as the operational algorithm. First multiply by the blade, then choose the grade that represents metric contact or span growth, and finally multiply by the blade inverse to return to the original geometric type. This prevents projection from looking like an unrelated formula.

slides.title: Mixed-Grade Inputs: Distribute First
slides.notes: The mixed-grade example is useful because it prevents a common overstatement. The grade formulas are cleanest for homogeneous factors. For general multivectors, split into homogeneous pieces, apply the retrieval rule to each pair, and then add the valid contributions back together.

slides.title: Symbolic Examples Worth Doing By Hand
slides.notes: Invite students to compute these examples aloud, because the signs reveal whether they understand ordering and orientation. The coordinate-plane example is especially instructive: a simple product can encode a turn, while the actual intersection line is better recovered through the dual meet construction.

slides.title: Proof Roadmap: Why The Grade Rules Work
slides.notes: Frame the proof as a filtering argument. Each time a vector is peeled from a blade, the possible grades are constrained. The selected component cannot receive contributions from the wrong grade, so induction turns the grade-selected expression into the familiar outer and contraction operations.

slides.title: Diagnostics: What To Check Before Naming A Product
slides.notes: This is the lecture's guardrail slide. The grade selector gives a reliable algebraic retrieval, but the geometric name still depends on grade, homogeneity, inverse placement, and duality convention. The notebook artifacts are designed as checks against exactly these mistakes.

slides.title: Takeaway: Products Are Stored, Not Replaced
slides.notes: Close by returning to the main intellectual payoff. Appendix C reduces the number of separate-looking operations students must carry. Once they can multiply, select grades, dualize when needed, and use blade inverses, they can retrieve the major subspace operations from one algebraic source.
